title: ERCOT prices at generator nodes
blurb: Real-Time Market settlement prices at 1,087 ERCOT generator settlement points for one 15-minute interval, 2:45 to 3:00 pm CT on Sunday, November 1, 2026. The Houston load zone settled at $73.66/MWh while North and West Texas sat near $11.
alt: Dark map of Texas with dots at generator locations on a continuous color scale from blue (negative prices) through teal and yellow to red ($170/MWh and up), over faint load zone outlines. North and West Texas dots are teal, near $10; South Texas dots are yellow-green, near $45; dots along the Houston Ship Channel are orange and red, above $100.

title: The Texas pipeline network
blurb: 365,000 miles of pipeline mapped by the Railroad Commission of Texas, 316,000 of them in service, colored by commodity. Gathering lines that collect oil and gas from wells make up 60% of the mileage and form the dense mesh in the Permian Basin and Eagle Ford.
alt: Dark map of Texas covered in a dense web of colored lines: natural gas in blue, crude oil in orange, NGLs in green, refined products in yellow, and CO2 in purple. Abandoned and removed lines appear as thin gray strokes, most visible along the Gulf Coast. The mesh is densest in the Permian Basin, the Eagle Ford, and around Houston.

title: Where America's solar farms are
blurb: 6,611 US solar facilities of 1 MW AC or more, 131.6 GW AC in all, grouped into hexagons by capacity and drawn as their real footprints over satellite imagery as you zoom in. Texas and California each hold about 17% of the capacity. Facilities under 10 MW are 77% of the count but 11% of the capacity.
alt: Satellite globe view of the contiguous United States covered in hexagons colored from dark purple (under 10 MW AC) to pale yellow (1,000 MW AC or more). The brightest hexagons are in the California and Arizona deserts, around Las Vegas, and in West Texas and Houston. Small purple hexagons fill the Northeast, Minnesota, and the Carolinas.

title: Every US power plant
blurb: Every operating US power plant in EIA Form 860M (September 2026), clustered on the map, with each ring showing the cluster's nameplate capacity by fuel. Gas is 41% of the 1,417 GW, while solar is 12% even though half of all plants are solar. Texas has the most battery storage, 19.4 GW to California's 16.5 GW.
alt: Dark globe view of the United States covered in donut-shaped clusters, each labeled with its total capacity, from 296 MW in northern Maine to 221 GW around Indiana and Ohio, with Hawaii's 3.7 GW at the left edge. Ring segments show the fuel mix: mostly coral gas across Texas and the Southeast, blue hydro in the Pacific Northwest, green wind on the Plains, and yellow solar with purple batteries in Southern California.

title: Within sight of a wind turbine
blurb: Where the blade tips of 1,666 wind turbines in Nolan and Taylor counties, Texas, are in line of sight from the ground, out to 25 miles, computed from USGS elevation data with earth curvature. At least one blade tip is in line of sight from 74% of the land within 25 miles of these turbines. Click a turbine to see its own viewshed, banded at 10 and 20 miles.
alt: Tilted 3D satellite view of the rolling ranchland around Sweetwater and Abilene, Texas, with a large rounded patch of color centered on two counties of wind farms. White dots mark 1,666 turbines in long rows along the ridges and mesas. The overlay shades each spot by how many blade tips are in line of sight from it: deep purple on the high ground near the turbine rows, where more than 1,000 tips can be in view, fading through red and orange to pale yellow at the outer edge, about 25 miles from the turbines.

title: The Permian Basin, 1958 and today
blurb: Four 1957–58 Army Map Service topographic sheets around Midland, Texas, which drew each well as a small circle, swiped against satellite imagery and the 447,665 wells on record in the same area today. The map opens on the Kermit and Wink oil fields in Winkler County.
alt: Swipe map split down the middle. On the left, a 1950s Army Map Service topographic sheet of Kermit and Wink, Texas, in pale green with red roads, labeled Winkler County Oil and Gas Field and Wink Oil Field, with hundreds of small open circles marking wells, along with pipelines, pumping stations and oil tanks. On the right, satellite imagery of the same tan ranchland today, crossed by caliche roads and well pads, with thousands of bright cyan dots marking wells.

title: Ten minutes from a fast charger
blurb: About 58% of Texans live within a 10-minute drive from a public DC fast charger, on 3.5% of the state's area. Drive times run outward from each of the 890 charging locations in and near Texas. Click anywhere or search a Texas town to draw your own 10-minute drive and count the chargers inside it.
alt: Light map of Texas with small teal shapes marking the area within a 10-minute drive of each public DC fast charging location, shown as dark dots. The shapes merge into large patches around Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin and San Antonio and run in chains along the interstates, while most of West Texas and the Panhandle is uncovered.

title: ERCOT, if every listed project gets built
blurb: Swipe between ERCOT's 182.6 GW of generating and storage capacity today and a grid where all 1,680 publicly listed projects in its interconnection queue get built, about 616 GW in all. Operating plants are filled dots and queued projects are rings, colored by fuel; most of the new capacity is solar and batteries.
alt: Dark swipe map of Texas split down the middle. On the left, filled dots for operating power plants, with wind in the west and gas, solar and batteries in the east. On the right, the same plants plus many more colored rings for queued projects, crowded across Central, East and South Texas and around Houston, mostly yellow solar and purple batteries. A legend lists capacity by fuel today and if all were built.

title: 153 million US jobs by sector
blurb: One dot for each of about 153 million jobs, placed at random within the census block where the job is recorded and colored by industry sector, from the Census Bureau's 2024 LODES workplace data. Michigan (2021) and Alaska (2016) use their latest available years.
alt: Dark map of the central United States covered in tiny colored dots, one per job. Dots cluster densely in Chicago, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Denver and Atlanta and thin out across the Plains. A legend lists 20 sectors from Agriculture to Public Admin.

title: The data center skyline
blurb: Data center building footprints from the IM3 Open Source Data Center Atlas (PNNL, from OpenStreetMap), stacked into 3D towers for 124 metro regions and colored by operator group. Northern Virginia holds 49.4M of the 235.2M sq ft mapped. Step the slider to rebuild the skyline for one operator group, or pick a hub to see its buildings in 3D. Built in R with mapgl from a single prompt in Claude Code, with no custom JavaScript. The prompt and the full R code are on the map.
alt: Dark globe view of the United States with hexagonal 3D towers rising from metro areas, each stacked in colors by data center operator group. The Northern Virginia tower is several times taller than any other, followed by Columbus, Dallas-Fort Worth, Hermiston, Atlanta and Phoenix. A panel on the left ranks the ten largest hubs and a legend lists eight operator groups.

title: The sound of Texas earthquakes
blurb: Monthly saltwater disposal at 10,884 Texas wells from the Railroad Commission's H-10 reports, with every cataloged M2.5+ earthquake inside Texas from USGS and TexNet, January 2015 through December 2025. Press play and each earthquake sounds as a timpani strike, lower and louder for larger ones. Injection grew from 4.37 billion barrels in 2015 to 7.77 billion in 2024, and earthquakes from 60 to a peak of 816 in 2022. Late 2025 reports are still coming in; wells not yet on file show as gray rings.
alt: Dark map of Texas with thousands of small cyan and violet dots for saltwater disposal wells, densest in the Permian Basin of West Texas, around Fort Worth and in East and South Texas. Orange dots and rings mark earthquakes, clustered heavily in the Permian Basin and along a band southwest of San Antonio. Gray rings mark wells whose late 2025 reports are not yet on file. A player panel at top right shows December 2025, 18.8 million barrels a day reported so far and 3,980 earthquakes.

title: The U.S. power grid, November 2026
blurb: Transmission lines and substations across the United States. The base is the HIFLD archive, which is no longer updated: 94,619 line segments as of September 2024 and 79,687 substations as of 2022. Added on top are 45,265 lines (66,425 miles) and 6,633 substations from a November 2026 OpenStreetMap pull that are not already in HIFLD. Line color shows voltage class; click a legend entry to filter, or press and hold one to show only that class.
alt: Dark map of the contiguous United States covered in a dense web of glowing transmission lines, mostly violet and purple for lines under 161 kV, with cyan 220-287 kV, green 345 kV and yellow 500 kV lines forming long corridors across the West and through the Southeast. A title panel at top left and a voltage class legend at bottom left.

title: Where Upton County's royalty owners get their mail
blurb: Click a survey and lines show where the owners on its Upton County, Texas mineral appraisal records get their mail. The map covers 248,795 royalty and overriding royalty records on the county appraisal district's 2026 mineral roll, 86% of the roll's total: the ones that name a single survey and have a mailing ZIP code that could be placed. That is 11,677 owners across 594 surveys, with addresses in 3,494 ZIP codes in all 50 states and D.C. About 64% of owners have a Texas address. Leases that cross the county line put 42 of the surveys just outside Upton, in Midland, Reagan and Crane counties. A panel counts owners, ZIP codes and states for the survey you pick and lists its most common mailing cities. Lines show appraisal records by mailing ZIP code, not income or ownership share.
alt: Dark map of the lower 48 states with thin teal lines fanning out from a circle in West Texas to hundreds of small white dots across the country, heaviest toward Houston and Dallas, with one long arc to Omaha. A panel at top left reads Survey A-486: 796 owners, 2,723 appraisal records, 477 mailing ZIP codes, 43 states, and 55% of owners with a Texas address, followed by a list of the most common mailing cities and a Reset view button.

title: Every mapped transmission tower in Texas
blurb: The 359,632 transmission towers in Texas that are mapped in OpenStreetMap, drawn as 3D models when you zoom in. Tower shapes and heights are illustrative, based on mapped tags and line voltage. Inspired by Jorge Luis Borges, “On Exactitude in Science.”
alt: Low aerial view over South Texas brush country with a row of white 3D lattice transmission towers, in pairs, running from the foreground toward the horizon and casting long shadows, beside a large electrical substation at lower right. A panel at top left reads Every mapped transmission tower in Texas, with buttons labeled Stand next to one and Back to Texas.

title: Inside the wells of Upton County, Texas
blurb: Click any of the 14,584 wells in Upton County, Texas to see it in 3D: the rock layers it passes through, where it was perforated, and the wells around it. 1,687 wells follow the directional survey filed for them with the Railroad Commission of Texas; the rest are sketches. The rock layers are a model built from formation tops that operators reported, not a geologist’s interpretation.
alt: A 3D block of ground in West Texas with its satellite-image surface lifted like a lid. Below it are colored rock layers labeled from Rustler to Wolfcamp, a depth scale to 10,000 ft, and a white well that runs straight down and then sideways for about four miles, drawn in orange where it was perforated. Thin white lines are neighbouring wells. A panel at top left reads Dorcus Cindy Kay (SA) E: depth 8,909 ft, length of the hole 30,160 ft, sideways reach 21,729 ft, with buttons labeled Back to the map and Another well.

title: Mapping a deed with AI in Land Intelligence
blurb: For the Collaborative prompt, a map that a person and AI make together. In Land Intelligence, AI reads a deed’s legal description, you check each call, and the tract is drawn over satellite imagery. Then export it as GeoJSON, KML or Shapefile. The screen shows a 0.72-acre parcel at the FM 1301 overpass in Wharton County, Texas, read from a Texas Department of Transportation parcel description. The curve in gold is one call from the deed, highlighted while it is checked against the deed’s own words. Land Intelligence is a research and drafting aid, not a survey.
alt: Screenshot of the Land Intelligence app. In the middle, satellite imagery of the edge of a Texas town, where a concrete overpass crosses a rail line. A blue dashed outline marks a parcel on the overpass, with one corner marked POB. An orange dashed line leads to that corner from a point marked POC, and one long curve along it is drawn in gold. A panel on the left gives the extracted deed: 0.72 acres, 8 calls, Wharton, Texas. A table on the right lists the eight calls, with the curve call’s words from the deed below it and a notice to check before saving.

title: The Permian Basin, day and night
blurb: Drag the bar to compare the Permian Basin by day and at night. By day it is desert, ranch land and well pads. At night the oil field is lit. White is light seen from orbit, from NASA’s Black Marble images. Orange marks places where a satellite saw heat on 3 or more nights in the past year, more than 800 of them in the Permian. In an oil field much of that heat is gas flares, but the satellite can’t tell a flare from a gas plant or a refinery.
alt: A map split down the middle by a drag bar. The left half is daytime satellite imagery of West Texas and southeastern New Mexico: tan desert with towns labeled from Carlsbad to Fort Stockton, scattered with small orange rings. The right half is the same region at night on a dark background: a wide patch of white light around Midland and Odessa, larger than the lights of Abilene and San Angelo to its east, dotted with orange points. A legend sizes the points by the number of nights heat was seen in the past year: 3, 30, 150 or more.

title: The 12,473 wells on Texas’s orphan list
blurb: For the NULL prompt, the Railroad Commission of Texas orphan list for October 2026. The Commission lists inactive wells whose operator’s state registration has been delinquent for more than a year, and color shows for how long. Hover a well for its type, depth, year completed and the last month its lease reported production, from Railroad Commission records compiled by Clearfork Intelligence. Click a row in the legend to hide or show that group. Another 197 wells on the list have no usable coordinates and can’t be drawn.
alt: A light gray map of Texas scattered with about twelve thousand small dots in pale orange, orange, pink, purple and dark purple. They are densest west of Fort Worth, around Abilene, near Pecos and Fort Stockton in West Texas, in the eastern Panhandle, and across South Texas between San Antonio and Corpus Christi. A legend gives the colors as how long the operator’s state registration has been delinquent, from 1 to 2 years (4,287 wells) to more than 20 years (448), with a last row for 197 wells with no usable coordinates.

title: Hydrogen sulfide in Texas oil and gas wells
blurb: For the Smell prompt: hydrogen sulfide, the gas known for its rotten-egg odor at low concentrations. Each dot is one of 153,770 wells on a lease with a hydrogen sulfide certificate on file with the Railroad Commission of Texas, colored by the concentration reported on the certificate, from 0 ppm recorded to more than 10%. The values are what the certificates report for the lease, not measurements of the air.
alt: A dark map of Texas with wells drawn as small dots in purple, teal, green and yellow. They cover the Permian Basin in West Texas, much of it green and yellow, a band across South Texas from the Rio Grande toward Victoria, the eastern Panhandle, and scattered patches in East Texas. A legend gives the colors as the hydrogen sulfide concentration reported on the lease’s certificate, from 0 ppm recorded (6,016 wells) to more than 10% (4,732 wells).

title: Well density in state oil and gas records
blurb: For the Hexagons prompt: more than four million wells and wellbores in the records of 32 state oil and gas agencies, counted in hexagons by how closely they are spaced. Producing, idle, plugged and dry holes are counted alike, and repeat records of the same well are grouped. Zoom in and the hexagons get smaller. State records also hold a small number of other wells, such as water and geothermal wells.
alt: A dark map of the contiguous United States tiled with hexagons shaded from dark purple to pale yellow by wells per square mile. The densest hexagons, in orange, run through the Appalachian Basin from western New York into West Virginia, across Ohio and Michigan, through Oklahoma and Kansas, the Permian Basin and East Texas, along the Gulf Coast and in California’s San Joaquin Valley. A legend runs from fewer than 0.1 to 100 or more wells per square mile; the pale yellow for 100 or more appears only when zoomed in.

title: What OpenStreetMap shows of Texas pipelines
blurb: Two maps of Texas side by side that move together. Left: every line tagged as a pipeline in OpenStreetMap, about 109,000 miles, colored by what its tags say it carries. Right: the Railroad Commission of Texas pipeline layer, about 316,000 miles in service. The two are made in different ways and do not count the same things, so each total describes its own source rather than scoring one against the other.
alt: Two dark maps of Texas side by side. On the left, OpenStreetMap’s pipelines, labeled 108,884 miles tagged as pipeline: a sparse web of lines, many of them gray for no substance tagged, densest along the Gulf Coast and in South Texas. On the right, the Railroad Commission of Texas layer, labeled 315,730 miles in service: a much denser web of blue natural gas lines with orange crude oil and green NGL lines, filling the Panhandle, the Permian Basin and the eastern half of the state. A shared legend gives the colors by what the line carries.

title: Where U.S. LNG went in 2025
blurb: The United States exported 5,509 billion cubic feet of liquefied natural gas in 2025, from the Energy Information Administration. Each line joins an export terminal to a country it sent gas to, drawn as a great circle on an Equal Earth projection, and each circle is sized by what that country received. The Netherlands received the most, 646 billion cubic feet. The lines are trade connections, not shipping routes.
alt: A dark world map on an Equal Earth projection. Thin blue lines fan out from a cluster of white terminal dots on the U.S. Gulf Coast: a thick bundle east across the Atlantic to Europe, where the largest gold circles sit, and other lines arcing to South America, the Middle East, India and East Asia. A legend gives circle sizes of 25, 200 and 600 billion cubic feet.

title: Corn into fuel
blurb: For the Taste prompt. The United States had 189 fuel ethanol plants at the start of 2026, with the capacity to make 18.4 billion gallons a year, from the Energy Information Administration. 175 of them were in EIA’s Midwest region. Gold shows the share of land mapped as corn in 2025 in the USDA’s Cropland Data Layer, a year when farmers planted 98.7 million acres of it.
alt: A light map of the contiguous United States with a broad gold band across the Corn Belt, from the Dakotas and Nebraska through Iowa, Minnesota, Illinois and Indiana into Ohio. Green dots mark ethanol plants, sized by capacity, packed into the same band and thinning out beyond it, with a few in Texas, California and the Southeast. Legends give the corn share from 3% to 60% or more and plant capacities of 50, 150 and 400 million gallons a year.

title: Electricity exchanges between grid operators
blurb: Electricity in the Lower 48 is managed by balancing authorities, each matching supply and demand in its own area. Each arrow is the net interchange reported between two neighboring authorities in September 2026, from the Energy Information Administration’s hourly Form EIA-930 reports, and points to the one that received more. Hover an arrow for how often it ran that way and what each side reported.
alt: A dark map of the United States with circles for the 60 U.S. balancing authorities and their Canadian and Mexican neighbors, placed near the middle of the areas they serve and joined by arrows shaded from dark teal to pale yellow. The widest, lightest arrows run from PJM toward MISO and New York, from MISO toward TVA, from Manitoba into MISO, and among the authorities of the Pacific Northwest, California and Arizona. A key reads net interchange reported, September 2026, with the largest at 3,163 GWh.

title: The Texas grid as a transit diagram
blurb: For the prompt Is this a map? 58 of Texas’s 345 kV substations drawn as stations on 9 colored lines, in the style of a transit diagram. Two stations are joined where the archived HIFLD data has 345 kV transmission lines running between them. It is not to scale, and it leaves out most of the grid.
alt: A transit-style diagram on a dark background: nine colored lines with white station rings, drawn only horizontally, vertically and at 45 degrees. The lines include Panhandle, West Texas, Dallas-Fort Worth loop, Houston loop and Coast and Valley, with stations such as Odessa, Parker, Zorn, Singleton and Rio Hondo. A key on the left lists each line and its ends.

title: Produced water disposal on the Texas side of the Delaware Basin
blurb: For the Water prompt. 885 disposal wells on the Texas side of the Delaware Basin injected 3.2 billion barrels of water in 2024, from Railroad Commission of Texas injection reports: 42% of all disposal reported in Texas that year. Numbered circles show where shared recycling hubs would sit to be closest to that water, found with the spopt R package. Move the slider to change the number of hubs from 3 to 10. Distances are straight lines, so this shows a method, not proposed sites.
alt: A light map of the Texas side of the Delaware Basin, outlined with a dashed line and filled with dots for disposal wells, each sized by the water it injected in 2024. With the slider at 5 hubs, the wells are colored in five groups, blue, green, red, purple and orange, each joined by thin lines to a numbered hub circle. A table gives the average miles from a barrel to its hub, from 11.6 with 3 hubs to 6.1 with 10.

title: What the map challenge added to mapgl
blurb: For the New tool prompt: mapgl, the R package behind this month’s maps. When a map needed something the package could not do, the package was changed instead of the map. Fifteen changes landed during the challenge, and thirteen grew out of work on the daily maps. Six have a small live map on the page, each using data from the day that needed it, and all fifteen are in mapgl’s development version.
alt: A page of six cards in a grid, each with a title, a line of R code, the challenge day it came from and a small live map: donut clusters of power plant megawatts across Texas, 3D wind turbine models on satellite imagery, a legend mixing a drive-time area and a circle over Dallas-Fort Worth, a jobs-by-sector legend over Houston, colored wells on a light map, and a flow map of electricity interchange across North America.

title: Energy bills as a share of household income
blurb: For the Feeling prompt: how much of a household’s income goes to electricity, gas and other home fuels, from the U.S. Department of Energy’s LEAD Tool estimates. Across the United States and Puerto Rico it is 2.3%. For households below the federal poverty line, their estimated average energy cost comes to 19.6% of their average income. Counties are shown when zoomed out and census tracts when zoomed in, and a search box finds an address.
alt: A light map of the contiguous United States with counties shaded from pale yellow to dark brown by the share of household income spent on energy. Darker counties stretch across the northern Plains from Montana through the Dakotas and Nebraska, through Appalachia and the inland South, and into Maine, with paler counties along the West Coast and around large cities. A legend runs from under 1.5% to 6% or more, with gray for no estimate shown, and a search box sits in the top right corner.

title: The cheapest path across a cost surface
blurb: For the Raster prompt: a cost surface of 100 meter cells between Kerrville and Brenham, built from public land cover, elevation, protected area and critical habitat data. The blue line is the cheapest path between two existing substations, found with route_corridor() from the spopt R package: 145 miles against 132 in a straight line, at 34% less modeled cost. It demonstrates a method and is not a proposed line.
alt: A raster map of Central Texas from Kerrville to Brenham, shaded from pale cream on open land to dark red-brown in Austin, San Antonio and other costly areas, with dark slate patches for land closed to the route. A dark blue line runs east from the Kendall substation to the Fayetteville substation, bending south of the dashed straight line between them, with two lighter blue alternatives looping north past Bastrop and south past New Braunfels. A legend gives the cost to cross from 1x to 100x or more against flat open land.
